Reprove

ri-PROOV · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To reprove to express disapproval of someone, typically in a mild or gentle way.

The librarian reproved the students softly, reminding them to lower their voices.

Worked Example

The coach reproved the young player quietly on the sideline, telling him to keep his temper in check next time.

A calm, private word of correction -- not a harsh public scolding -- is exactly what reprove describes.

How Strong Is It? — correct → reprove → rebuke

correct vs. reprove

correct vs. reprove: To correct someone is simply pointing out a mistake; to reprove them is to gently express disapproval of their behavior, not just the error itself.

rebuke vs. reprove

rebuke vs. reprove: Rebuke pushes further than reprove, implying a sharper, more direct expression of disapproval, often in front of others.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, again (Latin)

root — prove

root — prove: to test or demonstrate (Latin (probare))

Put it together

Put it together: re- ('back, again') + prove (to test or judge) together suggest examining someone's behavior again and finding fault -- the gentle correction reprove describes.

Use the root in a new word: approve

Use the root in a new word: approve: Approve shares the same Latin root probare ('to test, to prove worthy'), joined here with the prefix ad- ('toward').
